dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Account for cross-host clock skew when applying the age ceiling to the foreign-host branch (e.g. only trust local-clock age, or widen the ceiling margin / document the skew assumption).
evidence: `return time.time() - os.stat(lock_dir).st_mtime` (_mkdir_lock_age_s) uses the local wall clock
branch 4 reclaims a foreign-host stamp purely on age: `if fields["host"] != _host_identity(): return _mkdir_lock_age_exceeds_ceiling(lock_dir)` (lock.py:392-393)

The foreign-host case is precisely the shared-filesystem / cross-host scenario where the dir mtime originates on a different clock; docstring says 'we cannot observe that host's processes and our own locks prove nothing about its kernel' — nor about its clock.
docstring: 'the lock dir's mtime is the acquisition time — the quantity the stale ceiling is measured against' (lock.py:298-300)

_reclaim_mkdir_lock removes the owner file then rmdir, both best-effort: `os.remove(...)` then `os.rmdir(...)` each swallow OSError (lock.py:433-440) — a successful remove followed by a failed rmdir mutates the dir's entries, advancing its mtime
On the next poll iteration the owner file is now absent (branch 1) and the freshly-bumped mtime makes _mkdir_lock_age_exceeds_ceiling return False again
dropped.finding: The age ceiling on the foreign-host branch compares the lock dir's mtime (written by ANOTHER host on a shared filesystem) against the local wall clock via time.time(); cross-host clock skew can make the computed age exceed the ceiling for a genuinely-fresh foreign lock, reclaiming it early and breaking cross-host mutual exclusion — the exact invariant yaw-gravel-linen protects.
merged_from: _mkdir_lock_age_s's docstring asserts the dir mtime 'is the acquisition time', but a directory's mtime advances on entry add/remove; a partially-failed _reclaim_mkdir_lock (owner file removed, rmdir fails) refreshes the dir mtime to now, resetting the age clock and re-arming the full 1h ceiling — delaying the backstop it exists to guarantee.

dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm the 3600s age-ceiling reclaim on the foreign-host shared-filesystem branch (lock.py:392-393) cannot break a still-live remote owner's lock (clock-skew/long-hold safety), or gate it behind an additional cross-host liveness/lease signal.
evidence: lock.py:392-393: `if fields["host"] != _host_identity():` now returns `_mkdir_lock_age_exceeds_ceiling(lock_dir)` instead of the prior unconditional `return False`.

Docstring branch 4 (lock.py:361-365): 'we cannot observe that host's processes and our own locks prove nothing about its kernel ... refused until the age ceiling, then reclaimed so a shared-filesystem orphan cannot wedge forever.' — i.e. reclaim occurs with NO liveness signal on this branch.
Module docstring lock.py:7-18 establishes the mkdir leg as the portable cross-host/shared-filesystem mutual-exclusion window; breaking it over a live remote owner violates that invariant.
Age is derived from `os.stat(lock_dir).st_mtime` (lock.py:302), so wall-clock/mtime skew on a shared filesystem directly governs the reclaim decision.
Mitigations present: git gc gc.pid precedent, normal hold is seconds (~1000x margin), fail-closed on stat error, and a WARNING is logged on reclaim (lock.py:432).
dropped.finding: The new age-ceiling backstop reclaims a FOREIGN-host mkdir lock on a shared filesystem after 3600s with no positive proof the remote owner is dead, which can break mutual exclusion: if a live remote host holds the lock >1h (long operation, hung-but-alive writer, or negative clock skew / backdated dir mtime), a second host reclaims it and both may write the store concurrently.
scenarios: Two hosts share an NFS/CIFS store; host A holds the write lock during a long/hung-but-alive append for >1h; host B judges the foreign-host stamp aged-out and reclaims it, then both write concurrently.
Clock skew or a backdated lock-dir mtime on the shared filesystem makes a recently-acquired foreign lock appear older than the 1h ceiling, triggering an early reclaim of a live owner's lock.
